title: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Variability and the constancy of species”. Scope: Foraminifera, especially Peneroplis

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Integrative taxonomy can decisively test selected alleged species complexes with existing molecular and morphological records. Coverage is too uneven to settle Thompson's broad claim about many genera.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare named morphospecies and genera using genomic delimitations, environmental time series and within-lineage shell morphometrics, especially in Peneroplis. Morphological forms repeatedly intergrading within one reproducing lineage would support the claim; stable genetically distinct lineages would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The phrase 'temporary manifestations' can mean plasticity or life-cycle stages.

Type material and sequence records are rarely linked to the same individuals.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Whether named forms are temporary variants or lineages is a standard species-delimitation question, and planktonic foraminifera now have both image libraries and public sequences. Those data cover only part of the benthic diversity the claim invokes, and life-cycle series that would show one individual passing through several 'species' remain scarce. Where sequences and morphology can be paired, the contrast between ecophenotypes and lineages is sharp.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare morphometric clusters with genetic clusters for genera Thompson treats as variable, especially Peneroplis and planktonic groups with many named forms. The claim is supported where single genetic lineages occupy several named species or genera and morphology shifts within a life cycle; it is refuted where those names correspond to stable, reciprocally monophyletic lineages.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Peneroplis, the example in the text, has far less public genetic and culture data than planktonic globigerinids.

Cryptic species make the opposite error from ecophenotypes, so a single global test will not have one answer.
